opus-5.5.text:
I think it's mostly about timing. When ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022, I was around thirteen, just starting middle school. That's the age when you're figuring out how to learn and how to think about problems on your own. So for us, AI didn't arrive as a disruption to habits we already had. It was there while our habits were forming.

Older people, even people only five or six years older, often describe AI as "a new tool I had to adapt to." They already had a workflow: search engines, textbooks, asking teachers, and AI got added on top. For a lot of people my age, the first instinct when we don't understand something is to talk it through with a model. It's not a special occasion. It's like how people a bit older than us never really thought of the smartphone as a new invention. It was just the default.

It also changes how we relate to it. We're less in awe of it, and maybe also less afraid of it. We've seen it be brilliant, and we've seen it be confidently wrong. Over a few years you build an intuition for when to trust it, when to push back, and how to phrase things so you get something useful. That intuition isn't something you get from reading about AI. You get it from growing up arguing with it, using it for homework, for side projects, for just being curious at two in the morning.

And I think the biggest difference is what we imagine is possible. If you're fourteen and you can build a working app or run an experiment with a model's help, the barrier between "I'm a student" and "I'm a builder" gets very thin. A lot of my friends don't think they need to wait until university or a job to start making real things. That mindset, more than any specific skill, is what I'd call being AI native.

Of course, there's a flip side. It's easy to lean on it too much and skip the struggle that actually makes you learn. So being native doesn't automatically mean using it well. But it does mean it's part of how we see the world from the start, not something we had to switch into.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI’s place in young people’s lives to smartphones being a default, but it does not draw the specified parallel to internet natives or mention children teaching parents to use either technology.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to timing. People my age were born right around when the smartphone became normal, so we never knew a world without a touchscreen in our pocket. But the bigger thing is that ChatGPT came out when I was about thirteen. That's exactly the age when you start forming your own study habits, your own way of asking questions, your own sense of what work is. So AI didn't arrive as a tool I had to adapt to. It arrived at the same moment I was figuring out how to think, and the two got tangled together.

Older people, even people just five or six years older than me, learned to write an essay first and then met AI later. For them it's an assistant, something they compare against how they used to do things. For us there's no "used to." When I get stuck on a math problem, my first instinct isn't to open a textbook or wait for the teacher. It's to open a conversation and argue with the model until I understand it. That feels as natural as breathing, and I think that instinct is what makes us native rather than just fluent.

I'd also say we have a different relationship with being wrong. We grew up watching these systems confidently say things that turned out to be false, so we learned early to treat every answer, human or machine, as a draft to be checked. My parents' generation grew up trusting the encyclopedia. We grew up verifying the chatbot. That skepticism, combined with the reflex to just ask, is probably the real signature of my generation.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as natural to the speaker’s generation and contrasts them with older people, but it does not compare AI natives with internet natives or say children teach their parents to use either technology.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because we’re growing up with AI while we’re still forming our habits. We’re not all experts in it, but asking an AI a question, using it to explore an idea, or getting help with something we’re learning can feel pretty natural.

For us, AI isn’t just something that arrived after we’d already figured out how to study and work. It’s part of figuring those things out in the first place. That’s what I mean by being AI natives. It doesn’t mean we automatically know when it’s right, though—learning to question its answers is part of growing up with it, too.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because AI is becoming part of everyday life while we’re still growing up. We’re learning how to study, create things, and solve problems with it already there. So it feels less like a new technology we have to adapt to and more like part of the environment we live in.

But being an AI native doesn’t mean we automatically know how to use it well. We still have to learn how to ask good questions, check its answers, and make our own judgments. To me, that’s the important part: growing up with AI, while also learning when to trust it and when to think beyond it.

r001.rationale: The response describes growing up with AI and learning to use it critically, but does not compare AI natives with internet natives or mention children teaching their parents either technology.
